newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Small drop in French jobless surprises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Small drop in French jobless surprises.

text.p: French unemployment showed a surprise small drop in October, but the percentage out of work remained at a record 12.6 percent and economists predicted that the jobless total would stay high throughout 1997.
The number of unemployed fell in October by 12,000 or 0.4 percent from the previous month to 3,100,800, the Ministry of Labour reported on Monday. But the figure was up 5.3 percent year-on-year.
And the jobless rate, according to International Labour Organisation criteria excluding those who did any work at all, was unchanged at 12.6 percent.

The decline in the raw jobless total gave some comfort to the conservative government, striving to cut unemployment in the face of weak growth at a time when it is trying to push its austerity programme to allow France to qualify for European monetary union.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe, fighting growing unpopularity among voters, said the numbers were in the right direction but it was too early to draw conclusions from one month's data.
"It's encouraging but I will resist sounding triumphant," he told reporters on a visit to the northwestern city of Lille.
Private economists said at least two months of straight falls would be needed to suggest unemployment was on the wane.
"Despite the small fall in October, the underlying trend in unemployment appears steadily upwards," General Accident economist Andrew Milligan said.
The high unemployment was putting heat on the government to act -- "hence the recent hints by some French officials for a weaker exchange rate against the dollar," said Milligan.

Late last month, two Bank of France monetary policy council members and former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a fall in the franc's exchange rate against the dollar, saying it would spur export industries and help create more jobs.

The calls reflected a feeling in France that Germany's attachment to a powerful currency was imposing too high a toll on European economies in the run-up to monetary union, due in 1999, economists said.

But the debate over the franc's value ignored the core problem afflicting France's economy -- lack of flexibility in its job market reflected by high labour costs and inability to hire and fire easily, economists said.

The jobless figures prompted brief profit-taking in bonds before the market concluded the October drop was more likely a correction after two months of big rises and that it did not change the hopes for interest rate cuts in the near-term.
The drop "is more month-to-month volatility. I really don't think it signals a change in the overall deterioration (of the labour market)," said economist Sonja Gibbs of Nomura.

Economist David Naude of JP Morgan noted that unemployment had risen by nearly 70,000 over the previous two months "and here I think we're seeing the usual volatility, probably paybacks for the strong rises of the past months."

Unemployment has been languishing around 12.5 percent since the summer. The government forecasts growth of 1.3 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year and economists said this would be insufficient to push unemployment much below 12 percent throughout 1997.

"What's worrying is that the next couple of years are supposed to be recovery years for France, and if it stays around these levels, the next time there's a downturn, you'll end up at 13 percent or more," said one economist.
